name: Pedro Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or the government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the jobseeker team at the benefits office on Kingsway. I handle claims for people out of work, mostly under twenty-five, and I check they're doing their job search and set up their appointments. Where I can, I point them at apprenticeships, because that's how my dad got started. I'm still junior and I mix up the sanction rules sometimes, so my team leader Colin double-checks anything serious.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Lena, she's a dental nurse. My family has a bakery on the high street, three generations, and I've got a share in it from my grandad, which is where most of my savings sit. I help out on Saturday mornings at five o'clock, mostly the ovens. I use the AI chat thing at work now and then, when a letter is really tangled, but I check it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. That's about what I'd expect. Useful for some letters, not much more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and that's it, people got excited over nothing. At work I'd say let's focus on getting young people into real jobs. Online I'd not bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I keep my job and keep learning it. I'd still use the chat tool for a tangled letter now and then. Nothing in that picture really touches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Ask Colin to walk me through the sanction rules properly, because that's my weak spot. Keep the Saturday shifts at the bakery and keep saving with Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady job, family business behind me, money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a good day on the jobseeker team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a lad of nineteen I'd been seeing for months started a plumbing apprenticeship. His mum rang the office to say thank you. That's the bit of the job I'd do for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do any of them frustrate you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few, yes. Some of the lads don't turn up, and I believe in sanctions when they're fair. But mostly they just need someone to believe they can graft.

Let's focus on getting **young people** into real jobs.
think: I **keep my job** and keep learning it the normal way.
I'll use the **chat tool** now and then for tangled letters.
do: Ask Colin to walk me through **sanction rules** properly.
Keep the **Saturday bakery shifts** at five in the morning.
Keep **saving with Lena** as we do now.
feel: **Calm**, with a steady job and **family business** behind me.

fieldNote: He takes **pride in apprenticeships**, echoing his father's start.
He believes in **fair sanctions** but mostly in encouragement.
His **bakery share** gives security beyond the job and his savings.

steps.text: Ask Colin for a proper walk-through of the sanction rules
Keep working Saturday mornings at the family bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. Checking claims and writing letters is the job, so it'd come for us first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change things, and we need to make sure young people still get trades and apprenticeships. At work I'd say let's learn the new tools once they've proven they work. I'd not be shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd shrink the team and stop hiring juniors. I'm junior and not the sharpest on the rules, so I'd be nervous. The bakery's a backup, but I'd rather keep this job a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the tools are in and Colin's using them, I'd learn them properly, so I'm not the one left behind. I'd up my bakery hours to two days at weekends. And I'd keep the savings untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be checking where I stand every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the bakery as a backup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mostly hands-on. Kneading, shaping, ovens at five in the morning. Robots come slower to that. My dad would like me there more, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change what you'd tell the young people you see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A lot of the office jobs those lads might've got go too. Apprenticeships and trades would matter more than ever when office jobs go.

steps.text: Learn the new claims tools once Colin is using them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a shock. I'd not be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should've seen this coming and protected working people. I'd say families and trades are what get us through. I'd vote for whoever puts apprenticeships first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's gone. Checking claims is thinking work, and that's first in line. I'd want to be out before they push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bakery full-time within the year. I'd put some savings into a second oven so we can do wholesale to cafés, which my dad has wanted for years. Lena and I would wait on buying a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come around 2031. What about the bakery then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the scary bit. Three years later it could come for the bakery too. But people still like a baker they know. I'd hope that buys us something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad first. He'd say we've survived supermarkets, we'll survive this. I'm not sure he's right, but it'd help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more manageable, but still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to get young people into trades, so let's do it. At work I'd push for more apprenticeship referrals. I'd say it to my mates too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay a few years, learn the tools when they come, then move to the bakery. The extra time lets me get the bakery ready instead of rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start a proper baking qualification at the college, evenings. By year three I'd help my dad set up the wholesale side. I'd keep working at the office until the bakery could pay me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel more in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Lena and I would buy a small place near the bakery. That way I'd be close for the early starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools at the office in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. The tools are proven by then, and it'd help me last longer at the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's plan properly, especially for young people. At work I'd talk about apprenticeships. I'd not be panicking anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's safe for a good while. I'd keep learning it and use the tools once they're in. But I'd know it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the office for six or seven years and aim to be one of the better caseworkers. I'd marry Lena and maybe start a family. Then I'd move to the bakery around year seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's on my mind but not pressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kids, maybe in three years. I'd want them to grow up near the bakery like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your kids in the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. They might do something else. I'd let them choose, but I'd want my kids to know how to work with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one. There's no time to get the bakery ready or get young people into trades. What would help is the government putting real money into apprenticeships, and support for family businesses to grow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the young people. Young people are starting out in a world where office jobs might not exist. Someone needs to point them at the trades.

headlineQuote: Young people are starting out in a world where office jobs might not exist.
portrait: A **27-year-old jobseeker caseworker** on Kingsway, still mixing up sanction rules.
He takes **pride in apprenticeships** and uses AI only now and then.
A share in his family's **bakery** gives him a hands-on fallback and savings.
As AGI nears he'd **move to the bakery**, investing in a second oven for wholesale.
With ten years he'd **marry** and start a family before switching.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to get the bakery or young people ready.
